appraisal_events.evidence: Club members campaign against the duke (his wife dreyfusarde, the Rothschilds received, he half German), and on election day «à la surprise générale, l'obscurité triompha de l'éblouissement : Chaussepierre, deuxième vice-président, fut nommé président du Jockey, et le duc de Guermantes resta sur le carreau».
appraisal_events.explanation: One witnessed movement: the Jockey passes the duke over when the presidency was his by seniority and installs the obscure M. de Chaussepierre in his place, a reversal the narrator confirms wounded him («En réalité, il ne décolérait pas»).

appraisal_events.evidence: Bréauté is «assez mal reçu» for raising the Dreyfus affair, and Oriane dispatches the witticism he retails: «je trouve le mot carrément idiot. Si c'est ça que vous trouvez spirituel !», after which «Bréauté qui, se voyant contredit, commençait à lâcher pied».
appraisal_events.explanation: Oriane takes the exchange and Bréauté visibly gives ground, disowning the mot he was passing on; the narrator's sympathy for «le pauvre Bréauté, qui ne pensait jamais qu'à faire plaisir» keeps her severity from being straightforwardly endorsed.

appraisal_events.evidence: The duke declaims about Jewish bad faith and «une immense affaire nationale», while the narration records the «bel et bien» tic acquired since the election, his loose use of «ad hominem», and that of all the affair's misfortunes «il ne fût, en réalité, sensible qu'à un seul : son échec à la présidence du Jockey» — the parenthesis «le duc pensait naturellement à l'élection maudite de Chaussepierre» dropped inside his own tirade.
appraisal_events.explanation: A separate moment in which the narrator's verdict, not the club's, deflates the duke: his national principle is exposed as club vanity and his rhetoric as borrowed and imprecise.

status_effects.explanation: A publicly registered defeat before his own world: denied the presidency that was his turn, and left «sur le carreau» in favour of a nobody.
The narration's own verdict is harsh: his political indignation is shown to be a private grudge in disguise, and his verbal habits are mocked.
An unspectacular, penny-pinching man is elected president of the Jockey over a Guermantes, to the general surprise of the set that elects him.

One movement, recorded once: the woman who passed unnoticed at the Opéra and whose greeting Oriane had refused to return two years earlier is now the wife of the man the Jockey preferred to the duke, and the Guermantes are said to be preoccupied with the Chaussepierre — her standing rises with the election that humiliated them.
His conversational offering is badly received and then called idiotic; he retreats behind «le mot n'est pas de moi» instead of defending it.
Her interruptions land («ce n'est pas moi qui l'achèterai») and force Bréauté to yield the point, leaving her with the upper hand in the exchange.
